props.title: Krocodylus
props.initialSlug: Beware the Jaws of the Nile

sections.content: **Krocodylus** (2000) belongs to the wave of low-budget creature features that flooded direct-to-video markets in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Following in the wake of Lake Placid (1999) and **Anaconda** (1997), this Australian-American co-production attempted to capitalize on killer reptile hysteria but failed to match even the B-movie charm of its predecessors. The film's Northern Territory setting echoes superior crocodile thrillers like Dark Age (1987) and Rogue (2007), though without their grasp of local atmosphere or tension-building expertise.

sections.content: The early 2000s saw a surge in aquatic monster movies trying to replicate the success of **Deep Blue Sea** (1999). Films like **Krocodylus** (2000) and **Dinocroc** (2004) relied heavily on emerging CGI technology, often to their detriment. The practical effects expertise showcased in earlier creature features like **Alligator** (1980) gave way to cheaper digital solutions, marking a distinct downgrade in visual quality and believability. SUBHEAD: The Australian Monster Movie Tradition

Australia's rich history of creature features offers far better examples than **Krocodylus** (2000). **Razorback** (1984) demonstrated how to blend outback atmosphere with genuine menace, while **Black Water** (2007) proved that realistic crocodile threats could be more terrifying than exaggerated monsters. Even the modestly budgeted **Bait** (2012) managed to create more compelling aquatic tension, despite its unlikely shark-in-a-supermarket premise.
